1.name: PET
1.guidance: Rinse it out and remove the cap (recycle the cap separately if your program takes it).
1.note: Accepted by nearly all curbside programs.
funFacts: PET is the most widely recycled plastic in the world.
Recycled PET (rPET) is often spun into polyester fiber for fleece jackets and carpet.
A PET bottle can take around 450 years to decompose in a landfill.

2.name: HDPE
2.guidance: Rinse it out. Caps can usually stay on.
2.note: Accepted by nearly all curbside programs.
funFacts: HDPE can be recycled up to 10 times before its quality degrades too much.
It's resistant to many chemicals, which is why it's used for detergent and solvent containers.
Recycled HDPE often becomes plastic lumber, pipes, or playground equipment.

3.name: PVC
3.guidance: Not accepted curbside — it can contaminate other recyclables.
3.note: A few specialty recyclers take PVC — check local hazardous/special waste programs.
funFacts: PVC is sometimes nicknamed 'the poison plastic' because it can release harmful chemicals when burned.
It's the third most-produced plastic in the world, mostly for construction materials.
Its chlorine content makes it difficult to recycle alongside other plastics, which is why so few facilities take it.

4.name: LDPE
4.guidance: Skip the curbside bin — take clean, dry film plastic to a store drop-off instead.
4.note: Many grocery stores collect #4 bags and film for recycling even though curbside won't.
funFacts: LDPE was the first type of polyethylene ever developed, back in 1933.
Its flexibility and water resistance are why it's the go-to plastic for bags and wraps.
A single plastic bag can take up to 20 years to break down outdoors.

5.name: PP
5.guidance: Rinse it out. Double-check your local program accepts #5 before bagging it with recyclables.
5.note: Accepted in many areas but not universal — some towns still landfill #5.
funFacts: Polypropylene has a high melting point, which is why it's the plastic used for microwave-safe containers.
It's the second most widely produced plastic in the world.
Bottle caps are almost always PP, even when the bottle itself is a different plastic — worth separating them before recycling.

6.name: PS
6.guidance: Not accepted curbside, especially foam forms — it breaks apart and contaminates loads.
6.note: A few specialty drop-off programs recycle rigid (non-foam) #6 — foam almost never.
funFacts: Foam polystyrene is roughly 95% air, which is what makes it such a good insulator.
It can take 500+ years to decompose in a landfill.
Several cities and states have banned foam takeout containers outright because they're so hard to recycle.

7.name: Other
7.guidance: Mixed or unlabeled resins usually aren't recyclable curbside.
7.note: A small number of #7 items (like certain large bottles) have specialty take-back programs.
funFacts: #7 is a catch-all category for any resin that doesn't fit cleanly into 1–6, including bioplastics.
Some #7 plastics contain BPA, a chemical many reusable bottle brands now deliberately avoid.
Because it's such a mixed bag, almost no curbside facility can sort or process #7 material.
